blocks.text: Dataset shuffling randomizes the order in which training examples are presented to the model, a small sounding step that has a real, measurable effect on how well and how stably a fine-tuning run converges.
This is the final topic in dataset preparation, closing the loop from raw collected data all the way through to a dataset that is genuinely ready to feed into a training run.
1. Why Order Matters During Training

blocks.alt: An ordered dataset gets shuffled into a randomized order

blocks.text: A model updates its weights incrementally, batch by batch, based on whatever examples it sees in that batch. If those examples arrive in a predictable, non random order, the sequence of updates can push the model in ways that reflect the dataset ordering rather than the underlying task itself.
2. What Happens Without Shuffling

blocks.alt: Category A examples seen first, category B seen later, leads to order biased learning

blocks.text: A common real world scenario is a dataset sorted or grouped by category, all examples of one type appearing together, followed by all examples of another type. Training on this unshuffled order can cause the model to essentially learn one category, then partially forget it while learning the next, rather than learning all categories together in a balanced way.

blocks.title: This is not a hypothetical concern
blocks.content: Datasets pulled directly from a database export or collected in batches by category are frequently ordered this way by default, making shuffling a genuinely necessary step, not just a best practice.

blocks.text: 3. Shuffling at the Example Level

blocks.alt: Example one, two, and three get randomly reordered relative to each other

blocks.text: The most basic form of shuffling randomizes the order of whole examples, so that examples originally next to each other in the raw dataset end up scattered throughout the training sequence instead.

code.content:
import random

random.seed(42)
shuffled_dataset = dataset.copy()
random.shuffle(shuffled_dataset)

blocks.text: 4. Shuffling Within vs Across Epochs

blocks.alt: Using the same shuffle every epoch is compared against reshuffling each epoch

blocks.text: Shuffling once before training starts and keeping that same order for every epoch is simple, but reshuffling the dataset fresh at the start of every epoch, so the model sees a different order each time through the data, generally produces more stable training and reduces the risk of the model picking up on any residual pattern in a single fixed order.
5. Buffer Based Shuffling for Large Datasets

blocks.alt: A shuffle buffer fills from a data stream, then samples randomly from within it

blocks.text: For datasets too large to comfortably hold entirely in memory, a shuffle buffer approach fills a fixed size buffer from the incoming data stream, then randomly samples from within that buffer while continuously refilling it, approximating a full shuffle without needing the entire dataset loaded at once.

blocks.text: 6. Shuffling and Reproducibility

blocks.alt: A fixed random seed produces a reproducible shuffle

blocks.text: Using a fixed random seed when shuffling means the exact same shuffled order can be reproduced later, which matters for debugging a training run or comparing two experiments that should differ only in one deliberately changed variable, not in the incidental order examples happened to arrive in.
7. What Shuffling Does Not Fix

blocks.alt: Shuffling alone does not fix label errors, bias, or quality problems

blocks.text: Shuffling addresses ordering effects specifically, it does nothing to fix mislabeled examples, systematic bias in what the dataset covers, or general data quality problems, all of which are addressed by the cleaning, annotation, and deduplication steps covered earlier in this module, not by shuffling.
8. Shuffling in Distributed Training

When training runs across multiple machines or devices simultaneously, a topic covered more fully in the Distributed Training Techniques module later in this course, shuffling needs to ensure each worker receives a genuinely different, non overlapping portion of the shuffled data, rather than accidentally training on duplicate or missing examples across workers.
9. A Simple Shuffling Checklist

items: Confirm whether the raw dataset has any natural ordering, by category, by date, by source, that shuffling needs to break up
Reshuffle at the start of every epoch rather than reusing one fixed order throughout training
Use a buffer based approach if the dataset is too large to comfortably shuffle fully in memory
Fix a random seed when reproducibility across experiments matters

blocks.text: Worked Example

A team notices their fine-tuned classification model performs unevenly across categories, doing well on categories that appeared later in their raw dataset export and worse on ones that appeared earlier. Investigating, they discover their dataset was exported sorted by category, and their training pipeline had never explicitly shuffled it before training.

After adding a proper shuffle step, reshuffled fresh at the start of each epoch, and retraining, performance evens out considerably across all categories, confirming the earlier unevenness was a training order artifact rather than a genuine data quality or model capacity issue.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a dataset is already randomly ordered without checking how it was originally collected or exported
Shuffling once before training and reusing that same fixed order for every subsequent epoch
Treating shuffling as a fix for data quality or labeling problems it was never designed to address
Forgetting to coordinate shuffling correctly across workers in a distributed training setup

blocks.text: Practice

Check a dataset you have access to, or one you have worked with recently, for any natural ordering, by date, by source, by category, and consider what training order effects an unshuffled version of that dataset might produce.
Key Takeaway

Dataset shuffling breaks up any natural ordering in the raw data so a model learns from a genuinely representative mix of examples throughout training rather than being biased by whatever sequence the data happened to arrive in, and reshuffling fresh each epoch, with a buffer based approach for very large datasets, is the practical default worth building into any fine-tuning pipeline.
